questions.prompt: A Python Lambda function imports a large SDK and fetches secrets at module level, outside the handler. Which requests pay for that work?
choices: Every request, because the handler module is imported again for each invocation
Requests that land on a new execution environment: on every scale-out as well as after idle time. Their REPORT line carries Init Duration
Only the first request after each deployment
None of them; Lambda shares imported modules between all environments of a function
questions.explanation: Module-level code runs in the init phase, once per execution environment, before the runtime first calls GET /runtime/invocation/next. A burst that needs ten more environments pays it ten more times, and since 1 August 2025 that time is billed too.

questions.prompt: A handler raises ValueError. What does a synchronous caller of the Invoke API receive, and what happens to the execution environment?
choices: HTTP 200 with X-Amz-Function-Error: Unhandled and the runtime's error JSON (errorType, errorMessage, stackTrace) as the body; the environment stays warm for the next request
HTTP 500, and the environment is destroyed
HTTP 200 with an empty body; the error only appears in CloudWatch Logs
HTTP 429, because failed invocations count against concurrency
questions.explanation: The runtime catches the exception, posts it to /runtime/invocation/ID/error and calls next again. The platform returns that body with the function-error header and keeps the process: only timeouts, crashes and failed inits reset an environment.

questions.prompt: A function times out at 3 seconds. The very next request on it takes 900 ms, although the handler normally needs 20 ms, and its REPORT line has no Init Duration. Why?
choices: The timed-out handler was still running, and the next request waited for it to finish
Lambda throttled the next request for a moment after the timeout
Provisioned concurrency was being recalculated
The timeout killed the runtime process (a reset). The next invocation started a new one inside its own duration, a suppressed init, which REPORT does not label as Init Duration
questions.explanation: After a timeout the process is in an unknown state, so the platform kills it. The environment is reused, but its next invocation pays for the runtime start and module-level code as part of Duration. minilambda's dispatch() and invoke() do exactly this; the RIE does it too.

questions.prompt: A payment webhook returns TooManyRequestsException while a different function in the same account handles a traffic burst, and the webhook's logs show nothing for the failed calls. Which change protects the webhook?
choices: Raise the webhook's timeout
Increase the webhook's memory size
Give the webhook reserved concurrency: capacity set aside that the other function cannot take, at the cost of a hard cap at that number
Add a retry loop inside the webhook's handler
questions.explanation: Throttles happen in the frontend when a concurrency limit is reached, before any process runs, so the function cannot log them; the Throttles metric and the caller see them. Functions without reserved concurrency share the account's unreserved pool (1,000 per Region by default).

questions.prompt: A handler starts a background thread to flush metrics and returns at once. On Lambda the metrics arrive late or never; in a long-running local server they always arrive. What explains it?
choices: Lambda kills every thread after each response
The Python runtime disables threading
Between invocations the environment is frozen: the thread gets no CPU until the next event arrives, and never runs again if the environment is destroyed. Flush before returning, or use an extension
Outbound traffic is blocked after the response is sent
questions.explanation: Once the runtime calls next, the environment is frozen until there is another event. minilambda reproduces this with SIGSTOP and SIGCONT on the process group, and its freeze test shows a ticking thread stop between invocations and resume during the next one.

questions.prompt: Under the Runtime Interface Emulator the first REPORT shows Init Duration: 0.42 ms and a timeout comes back as plain text with HTTP 200. Why should you not size provisioned concurrency or alarms from these local results?
choices: The emulator runs one environment and its Init Duration measures only its own setup, with the real runtime start hidden inside the first Duration; it emulates no concurrency, freezing or Lambda error format. Measure init from REPORT lines on Lambda
The emulator's numbers are accurate; 0.42 ms means the imports were cached
The emulator only supports Python base images
Provisioned concurrency is sized by memory, not by init time
questions.explanation: The RIE checks the runtime contract and your handler, not the platform. For cold-start sizing use Lambda's own REPORT lines (Logs Insights @initDuration) or a platform like minilambda that models init, reset and concurrency.
